newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvia reforms safe despite PM resignation.
newsitem.headline: Latvia reforms safe despite PM resignation.

text.p: Reforms in the former Soviet republic of Latvia seem likely to stay on track despite the resignation of Prime Minister Andris Shkele although prolonged political uncertainty could harm the country.
Shkele announced on Friday he would quit on Monday following the recent resignation of several ministers amid corruption scandals. There was no indication who might succeed him.
Relations between the technocrat premier and the seven ruling parties had deteriorated since he accused them of pursuing their own selfish interests.
Shkele, an ex-businessman, was credited with giving impetus to the reforms and pulling Latvia out of a financial crisis caused by the collapse of its largest bank in mid-1995.
"We are not worried because there is broad-based consensus on the need for reforms," International Monetary Fund (IMF) Latvia representative Dimitri Demekas told Reuters.
"But if the political uncertainty is prolonged there is a risk of delay in structural reforms and questions about the 1998 budget, which is in an election year," he added.

The coalition, which has 73 seats in the 100-seat parliament, is a mixed bag ranging from nationalists to centrists and moderate leftists. They have already begun talks on choosing a new prime minister and the current government line up is expected to hold on to power.
Analysts say one of Shkele's key achievements was to push through a balanced budget in 1996 and 1997. He planned to pass deficit-free packages also for 1998 and 1999.
Moreover, he gave a push to privatisation, which seemed to have stagnated under the previous administration.
A stake has been sold in the state-owned gas company and offers are out for stakes in the state electricity supplier and shipping company.
Latvia, perched precariously with fellow Baltic states Estonia and Lithuania next to huge neighbour Russia, quit the former Soviet Union in 1991 and launched market reforms.
Shkele is credited by supporters with giving the image of Latvia a boost abroad and helping put it more firmly on the investment map.
"Shkele had generated respect as a successful and determined reformer, especially abroad, of which Latvia's credit rating was one sign," said stock exchange president Uldis Cerps.
Latvia gained an investment-grade credit rating by influential U.S. agency Standard & Poor's, higher than several of the star central and eastern European reformers.
"The course of reforms will probably not change drastically...but any unclear situation can influence the (stock) market in the short-term," Cerps added.
"The long-term affects will not be clear until we see the new government line-up," he added.
Market players were not expected to be jolted by the news.
"Instability is always bad...but it probably won't affect the market very much," said Andreta Petersone, an equities broker with Hansabank-Latvija.
"Reforms will have to continue," she added.
